blocks.title: Electric potential difference
blocks.text: The electric potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them: V = VB - VA = WAB / qo = dU / qo (16.1). Its SI unit is the volt: 1 V = 1 J / 1 C (16.2).

The volt can be scaled into kilovolts or millivolts. The potential difference is linked to the electric field by dV = E dd (16.3): the electric field is the rate of change of potential with distance, E = -dV/dd (16.4). The negative sign shows that the field points from higher to lower potential; in other words, the electric field at a point equals the negative of the potential gradient there. For a uniform field this simplifies to E = V/d (16.5). So the potential difference between two points is proportional to the field strength and to their separation: a stronger field gives a more rapid fall in potential. Fig 16.1 shows a positive test charge qo being moved from A to B against a uniform field between two charged plates.

blocks.alt: Left: two horizontal plates, positive on top and negative below, with vertical field arrows E pointing down; a positive test charge between points A (lower) and B (upper) has a green arrow pointing up, against the field. Right: a positive point charge +q with field lines radiating outward and two nearby points A and B on one line, a small distance dr apart.
blocks.caption: Potential difference in a uniform field, and the radial field of a point charge (original diagram after Figs 16.1 and 16.2).
blocks.long_description: In a uniform field the potential changes steadily (E = V/d). Near a point charge the field gets weaker with distance, so the potential is found by adding the work over many small steps, giving V = kq/r.

blocks.text: A 6 V battery is connected to two parallel copper plates 0.3 cm apart. Find the electric field between them. Solution: dV = 6 V and dd = 0.3 cm = 0.003 m, so E = dV/dd = 6 V / 0.003 m = 2000 N C^-1 (the same as 2000 V m^-1).

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: Although points at infinity are taken to be at zero potential, in practice the Earth is taken to be at zero potential. The absolute value of the potential at a point is therefore measured with respect to the Earth.
